title: Architecture — clean architecture, caching, microservices honesty
exp: Defend layering choices. Don't propose microservices for a simple CRUD app — interviewers reward honesty.
pts: Clean/onion: UI → Application → Domain ← Infrastructure; know where validation & transactions live.
Split services for independent deploy/scale/team ownership — accept distributed complexity.
Cache aside with Redis/`IMemoryCache`; plan TTL + invalidation; watch stampedes.
CAP: usually strong consistency in one DB, eventual across services.
SOLID as judgment tools, not religion.
pr: Sketch clean architecture folders for Orders
Design cache keys + invalidation for product pages

r: Deep dive into Day 12 runtime execution mechanics and threading constraints.
Focus on zero-allocation and lock-free patterns where applicable.
High concurrency contention or unexpected resource exhaustion under load.
Implement resilient backpressure, retries, and circuit breakers.
Balancing low latency, developer ergonomics, and system consistency.
Always state operational cost and complexity trade-offs.

qa.q: When are microservices the wrong choice?
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** Small team/domain, unclear boundaries, or when a modular monolith would ship faster with fewer failure modes. Microservices add network latency, consistency, and ops cost — justify with real scaling or team ownership needs.

**Under the Hood & Mechanics:** Operating When are microservices the wrong choice? at scale requires understanding the runtime lifecycle, memory allocations, and underlying execution constraints. The underlying framework or storage engine optimizes execution when contracts are explicitly preserved.

**Production Failure Mode & Gotcha:** Un-handled edge cases in When are microservices the wrong choice? under high concurrent traffic can lead to performance degradation, unhandled exceptions, or unexpected memory growth. Always enforce defensive validation and error handling.

**Senior Trade-Off Signal:** Choosing this implementation approach balances developer velocity and system performance. Senior engineers evaluate latency, operational overhead, and maintenance costs before committing.

qa.q: Describe cache-aside and one failure mode.
qa.a:
**Elevator Pitch:** App reads cache; on miss, loads DB and populates cache with TTL. Failure modes: stampedes on expiry, stale reads after writes without invalidation, and caching personalized/security-sensitive data incorrectly.
